definition: spreading through every part of something

hero.text: A pervasive smell of smoke filled every room of the building, so Kai knew the fire was spreading through the vents.

everyday: The novel captures the pervasive fear in the town during the long, cold war years.

contrast.nonExample: There was a small coffee stain in one corner of the tablecloth.
contrast.explanation: A small stain in one spot is limited. Pervasive describes something that spreads throughout.

items.prompt: What does "pervasive" mean in this sentence?
items.passage: There was a pervasive sense of excitement throughout the school during the week before the championship.
items.hint: Notice "throughout the school."
items.explanation: Pervasive means spreading through every part of something. The excitement was felt "throughout the school."

items.prompt: Choose the word that best completes the passage.
items.passage: In the 1930s Dust Bowl, the dust was so ___ that families found it in their food, their beds, and even inside closed cupboards.
items.hint: The dust got into everything.
items.explanation: Dust that got into food, beds, and closed cupboards had spread throughout every space: it was pervasive.
items.clue: in their food, their beds, and even inside closed cupboards

items.prompt: Which word best describes the problem?
items.passage: The investigation found that cheating was not limited to one class or grade. It appeared in every subject, at every level, and in clubs and sports as well.

wrong.b: Isolated is the opposite: confined to one spot.
wrong.d: Minor means small in importance; the problem is widespread.
wrong.a: Cheating on this scale is not described as accidental.

items.hint: "Not limited to one class," but in every part of the school.
items.explanation: A problem found in every subject, level, and activity is pervasive. Isolated would mean it was limited to one place.

items.prompt: Which word means the OPPOSITE of "pervasive" in this sentence?
items.passage: The report described a pervasive culture of secrecy inside the agency.
items.hint: Which word means "confined to a small area"?
items.explanation: Pervasive means spread throughout. Limited means confined, the opposite. Widespread is a synonym.

items.prompt: Is the influence described pervasive?
items.passage: Social media now shapes how teenagers shop, talk, study, make friends, and even how they see themselves.
items.hint: Does the influence reach into many parts of life?
items.explanation: Yes. An influence that reaches shopping, talking, studying, friendships, and self-image spreads throughout life: it is pervasive.

definition: to divide people into two sharply opposing groups

hero.text: The debate over secret identities polarized the academy: half the heroes wanted masks, half wanted to go public.

everyday: The proposal to cancel the school trip polarized parents, with some strongly for it and others strongly against.

contrast.nonExample: The class discussed the new schedule and quickly agreed it was an improvement.
contrast.explanation: Quick agreement unites people. Polarizing pushes them toward two opposite extremes.

items.prompt: What does "polarized" mean in this sentence?
items.passage: The controversial painting polarized critics: some called it a masterpiece, while others called it an insult to art.
items.hint: "Masterpiece" versus "insult." How far apart are these views?
items.explanation: Polarize means divide into two sharply opposing groups. Critics split into strong admirers and strong haters.

items.prompt: Choose the word that best completes the passage.
items.passage: The question of slavery increasingly ___ the United States in the 1850s, until the North and South could no longer find any compromise.

wrong.c: United is the opposite of what happened.
wrong.d: Enriched means made richer or better.
wrong.a: Surprised describes a reaction, not division.

items.hint: Two sides moving so far apart that no compromise was possible.
items.explanation: When two regions can no longer compromise, the issue has polarized them, pushing them to opposite extremes.
items.clue: North and South could no longer find any compromise

items.prompt: Which word best describes the effect of the new dress code?
items.passage: Before the vote, most students felt neutral about the dress code. After a heated assembly, nearly everyone was either passionately for it or passionately against it.

wrong.d: Being informed does not explain the split into extremes.
wrong.a: Persuaded suggests everyone moved toward one view; instead, they split.
wrong.b: Calmed is the opposite of a heated split.

items.hint: From neutral to two extremes.
items.explanation: Moving from neutral to two strongly opposed camps means the issue polarized students. Persuaded would mean they moved toward one side.

items.prompt: Build a sentence that shows what polarize means.

chunks.text: splitting residents into two angry camps.
bringing every neighbor together in agreement.

items.hint: Polarizing divides people into opposing sides.
items.explanation: Splitting residents into two angry camps shows polarization. Bringing everyone together is the opposite.

items.prompt: Which word means the OPPOSITE of "polarize" in this sentence?
items.passage: Leaders should look for solutions that unite communities rather than polarize them.
items.hint: Which word means "bring together"?
items.explanation: Polarize means divide into opposing groups. Unify means bring together, the opposite. Divide and split are close synonyms.

definition: an earlier event or decision used as an example or rule for similar situations later

hero.text: When Pixel let a civilian help with a rescue, Rex worried it would set a precedent for every future mission.

everyday: The court's ruling set a precedent that other judges followed in similar cases for decades.

contrast.nonExample: Every year, the class plants a tree on the first day of spring, just as the school has always done.
contrast.explanation: Following an old tradition is not the same as setting a precedent. A precedent is the earlier example that guides later decisions.

items.prompt: What does "precedent" mean in this sentence?
items.passage: George Washington set a precedent by stepping down after two terms, and most presidents followed his example for the next 150 years.

options.text: a written law passed by Congress
an earlier example that others follow
a final decision that ends a debate

items.hint: "Most presidents followed his example."
items.explanation: A precedent is an earlier action used as a model for later ones. Later presidents followed Washington's example.

items.prompt: Choose the word that best completes the passage.
items.passage: The principal hesitated to let one student retake the exam, worried that the exception would become the ___ every student would then expect to follow.

wrong.d: A retake is not a punishment.
wrong.a: The concern is about future expectations, not a question.
wrong.b: It might be a mistake, but the specific worry is that it becomes a model.

items.hint: One exception could become a model for future requests.
items.explanation: Allowing one retake could become an example others expect to follow: a precedent.
items.clue: every student would then expect to follow

items.prompt: "Precedent" comes from "pre-" (before) and "ced" (go), like "precede." What does that suggest?

options.text: something that goes after everything else
something that goes before and guides what follows

items.hint: "Pre-" means before, as in "preview."
items.explanation: A precedent "goes before": it is an earlier example that later decisions follow.

items.prompt: Which word best completes the sentence?
items.passage: Lawyers searched old court records for a ___ in which a judge had ruled on a similar dispute about a shared fence.

wrong.b: A verdict is the decision in a case; lawyers want an earlier verdict that can serve as a model, which is a precedent.
wrong.c: A witness gives testimony, not a guiding ruling.
wrong.d: A statute is a law passed by a legislature, not a past court ruling.

items.hint: They want an earlier case to guide this one.
items.explanation: An earlier similar ruling that can guide the current case is a precedent. A verdict is just a decision in one case, and a statute is a written law.

items.prompt: Does this describe setting a precedent?
items.passage: The first time the student council allowed a club to raise money by selling snacks, other clubs began asking for the same permission.
items.hint: Did the first decision become an example for later requests?
items.explanation: Yes. The first approval became an example that other clubs pointed to, so it set a precedent.

definition: the art of using language to persuade; also, persuasive language that may sound impressive but lack substance

hero.text: Nova's speech used powerful rhetoric, with repetition and vivid images, to convince the city to rebuild together.

everyday: In debate class, students study rhetoric, including how speakers appeal to logic, emotion, and trust.

contrast.nonExample: The instruction manual listed the steps to assemble the shelf, one by one.
contrast.explanation: A plain set of instructions is not trying to persuade, so it is not rhetoric.

items.prompt: What does "rhetoric" mean in this sentence?
items.passage: Martin Luther King Jr.'s rhetoric, with its repetition of "I have a dream," moved millions of listeners.
items.hint: The repeated phrase "moved millions."
items.explanation: Rhetoric is the art of using language to persuade or move an audience, here through repetition.

items.prompt: What is the writer's view of the candidate's speech?
items.passage: The candidate's speech was full of soaring rhetoric about "a brighter tomorrow," but voters noticed it contained no actual plan for jobs or schools.

options.text: It sounded impressive but lacked substance.
It was boring and poorly delivered.
It was too short to judge.

wrong.b: "Soaring" suggests it was impressive, not boring.
wrong.c: The passage says it had no actual plan.

items.hint: "Soaring" language, "but" no actual plan.
items.explanation: Here rhetoric means impressive-sounding language without substance. The speech sounded grand but had no plan.

items.prompt: Choose the word that best completes the passage.
items.passage: In ancient Athens, citizens studied ___ so they could argue persuasively in the assembly and defend themselves in court.
items.hint: Which subject teaches persuasive speaking?
items.explanation: Rhetoric is the study of persuasive language, exactly what citizens needed to argue in the assembly and in court.

items.prompt: Which word best describes the speaker's technique?
items.passage: "Will we stand by and do nothing? Will we let our park disappear? Or will we act?" the speaker asked, pausing after each question.
items.hint: The questions are meant to persuade, not to get answers.
items.explanation: Questions asked to stir the audience rather than get answers are a tool of rhetoric. Evidence and statistics would be facts or numbers, which this passage lacks.

items.prompt: Which speaker uses "rhetoric" correctly?

options.text: "The rhetoric fell off the shelf and broke."
"We went swimming in the rhetoric after school."
"Her rhetoric was so persuasive that the whole class changed its vote."

items.hint: Rhetoric is persuasive language.
items.explanation: Rhetoric is persuasive language, so "her rhetoric was so persuasive" uses it correctly. The other lines treat it as a food, an object, or a place.

definition: humor, exaggeration, or irony used to criticize or mock people's foolishness or faults, especially in society or politics

hero.text: Pixel's cartoon showing the mayor as a snail racing to fix potholes was a sharp satire of the city's slow repairs.

everyday: Jonathan Swift wrote a famous satire suggesting that the poor sell their children as food, mocking cruel attitudes toward the poor.

contrast.nonExample: The comedian told jokes about his dog chasing its own tail.
contrast.explanation: Silly jokes for fun are not satire. Satire uses humor to criticize a fault or a foolish idea.

items.prompt: What does "satire" mean in this sentence?
items.passage: The TV show is a satire of reality television, exaggerating the drama to show how fake those programs can be.
items.hint: It exaggerates in order to criticize.
items.explanation: Satire uses humor and exaggeration to criticize. The show mocks how fake reality television can be.

items.prompt: Is this an example of satire?
items.passage: A school newspaper prints a fake article announcing that the cafeteria will now serve "gourmet cardboard," poking fun at the poor quality of school lunches.
items.hint: Does it use humor to criticize something?
items.explanation: Yes. The fake article exaggerates to criticize school lunches, which is satire.

items.prompt: Which word best names this kind of writing?
items.passage: In the story, a government hires 500 officials to study why it takes so long to make decisions; after ten years, they announce they need more time.
items.hint: The story mocks government inefficiency with absurd exaggeration.
items.explanation: The story exaggerates bureaucratic slowness to mock it, so it is satire. A tragedy would be a serious story ending in disaster.

items.prompt: Choose the word that best completes the passage.
items.passage: In Animal Farm, George Orwell uses ___ to mock the corruption of the Soviet government: farm animals overthrow their owner, only to be ruled by pigs who become just as cruel and ridiculous.
items.hint: Which tool is used to mock and criticize?
items.explanation: Using an absurd animal fable to mock political corruption is satire. Statistics, footnotes, and diagrams are tools for presenting facts, not for mocking.
items.clue: to mock the corruption; just as cruel and ridiculous

items.prompt: What is the cartoonist's purpose?
items.passage: A cartoon shows tech executives building a huge "Save the Planet" billboard powered by a smoking coal generator.
items.hint: Notice the contradiction between the message and the power source.
items.explanation: The cartoon uses irony (a planet-saving sign powered by coal) to mock hypocrisy. That is satire.

definition: to combine separate ideas, information, or elements into a new whole

hero.text: Juniper synthesized clues from three different witnesses into one clear map of the villain's escape route.

everyday: For her research paper, Mei synthesized findings from five different studies into one argument about sleep and memory.

contrast.nonExample: Leo copied one paragraph from a single website into his report.
contrast.explanation: Copying a single source does not combine anything. Synthesizing brings several sources together into something new.

items.prompt: What does "synthesize" mean in this sentence?
items.passage: The historian synthesized letters, diaries, and newspaper reports to create a complete picture of life during the war.

options.text: to combine into a new whole

items.hint: Several sources become one complete picture.
items.explanation: Synthesize means combine separate parts into a new whole. The historian combined three kinds of sources into one picture.

items.prompt: Choose the word that best completes the passage.
items.passage: Plants ___ sugar from carbon dioxide, water, and sunlight during photosynthesis.

wrong.c: Plants take in these ingredients; they do not reject them.
wrong.d: Freezing has nothing to do with photosynthesis.
wrong.a: Plants release oxygen, but sugar is built, not released.

items.hint: Separate ingredients are combined into a new substance.
items.explanation: Plants combine carbon dioxide and water, using light energy, into sugar: they synthesize it. The word even appears inside "photosynthesis."
items.clue: from carbon dioxide, water, and sunlight

items.prompt: Which word best describes Nia's task?
items.passage: Nia's teacher asked her not just to summarize each article separately, but to combine their main ideas into a single new argument.

wrong.c: The teacher specifically asked for more than separate summaries.
wrong.a: Criticizing means judging faults, not combining.
wrong.b: Memorizing would not create a new argument.

items.hint: She must combine ideas, not just retell each one.
items.explanation: Combining main ideas from several sources into one argument is synthesizing. Summarizing would only shorten each source on its own.

items.prompt: Which word means the OPPOSITE of "synthesize" in this sentence?
items.passage: Good researchers synthesize information from many sources.
items.hint: Which word means "break apart"?
items.explanation: Synthesize means bring parts together. Separate means break them apart, the opposite. Integrate and combine are synonyms.

items.prompt: Build a sentence that shows what synthesize means.

chunks.text: synthesized jazz rhythms and classical melodies
into a completely new style of music.
by deleting every note from both styles.

items.hint: Synthesizing combines elements into something new.
items.explanation: Blending jazz and classical into a new style is synthesizing. Deleting notes destroys rather than combines.

definition: never having happened or existed before

hero.text: Bolt's rescue of an entire falling train was unprecedented: no hero had ever attempted anything like it.

everyday: The pandemic caused unprecedented school closures, with nearly every school in the country closing at once.

contrast.nonExample: Our town has a parade every Fourth of July, just as it has for a hundred years.
contrast.explanation: An event that happens every year is familiar. Unprecedented means it has never happened before.

items.prompt: What does "unprecedented" mean in this sentence?
items.passage: The 1969 moon landing was an unprecedented achievement: no human had ever stood on another world.
items.hint: "No human had ever..."
items.explanation: Unprecedented means never having happened before. No one had ever walked on the moon.

items.prompt: "Unprecedented" combines "un-" (not) with "precedent" (an earlier example). What does the word mean?
items.hint: If there is "not" any earlier example, what does that tell you?
items.explanation: Un- means not. Something unprecedented has no precedent, no earlier example of anything like it.

items.prompt: Choose the word that best completes the passage.
items.passage: Scientists recorded ___ ocean temperatures last summer, higher than any reading since measurements began in the 1800s.
items.hint: "Higher than any reading" ever taken.
items.explanation: Temperatures higher than any ever recorded are unprecedented. Average or seasonal would mean typical.
items.clue: higher than any reading since measurements began

items.prompt: Is this event unprecedented?
items.passage: For the fifth year in a row, the school's robotics team qualified for the state finals.
items.hint: Has this happened before?
items.explanation: No. It has happened four times before, so it is not unprecedented. An unprecedented event has never happened before.

items.prompt: Which word best describes the election result?
items.passage: For the first time in the country's 200-year history, a candidate from outside the two major parties won the presidency.

wrong.b: It may have been controversial, but the passage emphasizes that it was a first.
wrong.c: A first-ever result is the opposite of predictable.
wrong.d: The candidate won, so popularity is not the issue.

items.hint: "For the first time in... 200-year history."
items.explanation: Something happening for the first time in 200 years is unprecedented. It may also be controversial, but the passage stresses that it never happened before.

definition: using more words than are needed

hero.text: Rex's mission briefing was so verbose that by the time he finished, the villain had already escaped.

everyday: The editor cut the verbose introduction from three pages to a single sharp paragraph.

contrast.nonExample: Her text message said simply: "Running late. There in 10."
contrast.explanation: A short, efficient message is concise, the opposite of verbose.

items.prompt: What does "verbose" mean in this sentence?
items.passage: The verbose instructions used three paragraphs to explain how to press a single button.
items.hint: Three paragraphs for one button.
items.explanation: Verbose means using more words than needed. Three paragraphs for one button is far too many.

items.prompt: Which word best describes the student's answer?
items.passage: Question: "What is the capital of France?" Student's answer: "Well, after careful consideration of the many cities in that historic nation, and keeping in mind various factors, I would say that the capital is, in fact, Paris."

wrong.d: Eloquent speech is graceful and effective; this answer is just padded.
wrong.a: Nothing in the answer is impolite.

items.hint: The answer is correct but uses far too many words.
items.explanation: The answer is right but padded with unnecessary words, so it is verbose. Eloquent means expressive and graceful, which this rambling answer is not.

items.prompt: Choose the word that best completes the passage.
items.passage: Journalists are trained to avoid ___ writing, since readers often skim and may stop reading if a story takes too long to get to the point.
items.hint: What kind of writing takes too long to get to the point?
items.explanation: Writing that takes too long to get to the point is verbose. Journalists value concise writing.
items.clue: takes too long to get to the point

items.prompt: Which word means the OPPOSITE of "verbose" in this sentence?
items.passage: The judge asked the lawyer to be less verbose and simply state the facts.
items.hint: Which word means "brief and to the point"?
items.explanation: Verbose means wordy. Concise means brief and clear, the opposite. Long-winded is a synonym.

items.prompt: Which reply is the most verbose?
items.passage: Jake asks his sister, "Did you feed the dog?"

options.text: "Regarding the question of whether the dog, our beloved family pet, has been fed this evening, I am pleased to report that yes, I did so."

items.hint: Find the reply with far more words than needed.
items.explanation: The third reply uses a whole paragraph to say "yes," so it is verbose. This is a rare case where the longest option is the answer, because length is the point.

definition: to prove that someone or something was right or innocent after being doubted or blamed

hero.text: When the security footage showed the real thief, it vindicated Kai, who had been wrongly accused.

everyday: Years after critics laughed at her theory, new fossil evidence vindicated the scientist.

contrast.nonExample: The team captain was praised for scoring the winning goal.
contrast.explanation: Praise for success is not vindication. To vindicate is to clear someone who was doubted or blamed.

items.prompt: What does "vindicated" mean in this sentence?
items.passage: Everyone said Ana's idea to build the bridge farther upriver was foolish, but when the flood washed away the old bridge and hers survived, she was vindicated.

options.text: shown to be right after being doubted

items.hint: People doubted her, then events proved her right.
items.explanation: Vindicate means to prove someone right after doubt or blame. The flood proved Ana's idea had been wise.

items.prompt: Choose the word that best completes the passage.
items.passage: After spending fifteen years in prison for a crime he did not commit, the man was finally ___ when DNA testing identified the real criminal.

wrong.b: Convicted means found guilty, the opposite.
wrong.c: Sentenced is what happened before the DNA test.
wrong.d: Suspected means doubted; the test cleared him.

items.hint: New evidence cleared him.
items.explanation: DNA evidence proved his innocence, so he was vindicated. Convicted and sentenced describe what happened before, not the clearing of his name.
items.clue: a crime he did not commit; identified the real criminal

items.prompt: Which word best describes how the engineer felt?
items.passage: For months, managers ignored the engineer's warnings about the faulty part. When an inspection confirmed the flaw, she felt quietly ___ rather than angry.
items.hint: Her doubted warnings were finally proven correct.
items.explanation: Being proven right after being ignored is feeling vindicated. Rewarded would mean receiving a prize or payment, which is not mentioned.

items.prompt: Which word means the OPPOSITE of "vindicate" in this sentence?
items.passage: The new evidence may vindicate the accused student.
items.hint: Which word means "make someone look guilty"?
items.explanation: Vindicate means clear someone of blame. Incriminate means make someone appear guilty, the opposite. Clear and justify are close to vindicate.

items.prompt: Is this person vindicated?
items.passage: Dev predicted the team would lose by a lot. They did lose, and nobody had argued with him about it.
items.hint: Was Dev doubted or blamed first?
items.explanation: No. Vindication means being proven right after being doubted or blamed. Nobody doubted Dev, so being correct here is not vindication.

definition: very careful to be accurate, honest, and do what is right, even in small details

hero.text: Pixel was scrupulous about recording every detail of the evidence, down to the exact time and position of each clue.

everyday: The scrupulous shopkeeper chased a customer down the street to return the extra dollar he had overpaid.

contrast.nonExample: Rafa rushed through the lab report, guessing some measurements to finish faster.
contrast.explanation: Guessing and rushing is careless. A scrupulous person is careful and honest about every detail.

items.prompt: Which person is scrupulous?

options.text: Kenji double-checks every source in his essay and credits each one exactly.
Pia copies a friend's math answers to save time.
Ty guesses at the measurements instead of using the ruler.
Ivy rounds her test results to make the experiment look more successful.

items.hint: Look for someone who is careful, accurate, and honest.
items.explanation: Kenji is careful and honest about every detail, which is scrupulous. The others are careless or dishonest.

items.prompt: Choose the word that best completes the passage.
items.passage: The restorer the museum hired was ___: she spent two years cleaning the painting with tiny brushes, documenting every square inch before touching it.

wrong.b: Hasty means rushed, the opposite of two careful years.
wrong.c: Fame is not shown by the details given.

items.hint: Two years and every square inch documented.
items.explanation: Extreme care and attention to every detail make the restorer scrupulous. Famous may be true, but it does not explain the careful method.
items.clue: spent two years; documenting every square inch

items.prompt: Which word best describes the treasurer?
items.passage: The club treasurer records every penny, keeps every receipt, and once reported her own small math mistake to the group, even though no one would have noticed it.

wrong.c: Stingy is about refusing to spend money, not about accuracy and honesty.
wrong.d: Nothing suggests she is worried; she is careful.
wrong.a: Generous means giving freely, which is not described.

items.hint: She is careful and honest, even when no one is watching.
items.explanation: Careful records and honestly reporting her own error show she is scrupulous. Stingy means unwilling to spend money, which is about spending, not honesty.

items.prompt: Which word means the OPPOSITE of "scrupulous" in this sentence?
items.passage: The scientist was scrupulous in following the safety procedures.
items.hint: Which word means "not paying attention to details"?
items.explanation: Scrupulous means very careful. Careless is the opposite. Meticulous and thorough are synonyms.

items.prompt: Build a sentence that shows what scrupulous means.

chunks.text: checked every quote with the original speaker
before the article went to print.
and invented a few more to make the story exciting.

items.hint: A scrupulous person is careful and honest.
items.explanation: Checking every quote before printing shows careful honesty. Inventing quotes is dishonest, the opposite of scrupulous.
